gaps.sentence: The author ___ books sell millions worldwide lives in Iceland.
gaps.explanation: 'Whose' links the author to her books; 'who' could not be followed directly by 'books'.

gaps.sentence: The author, about ___ there has been much debate, will speak at the festival.
gaps.hint: debate about the author — person after preposition
gaps.explanation: 'About whom' is required after the preposition 'about' when referring to a person.

gaps.sentence: The director, ___ we met at the conference, has written to us.
gaps.hint: person as object, but the clause is non-defining
gaps.explanation: In non-defining clauses 'that' cannot replace 'who', even when the person is the object.

gaps.sentence: This clock, ___ belonged to my grandmother, is still working perfectly.
gaps.hint: thing as subject; clause between commas
gaps.explanation: The clock is a thing, so 'which' is correct; 'that' cannot be used in a non-defining clause.

gaps.hint: after 'all', the relative pronoun is not 'what'
gaps.explanation: 'All that glitters' is the proverb pattern; 'what' cannot follow 'all', and 'which' is avoided after 'all'.

gaps.sentence: Nobody knows the reason ___ he resigned so suddenly.
gaps.explanation: 'The reason why ...' is the standard pattern; 'why' means 'for which'.

gaps.sentence: He passed all his exams first time, ___ surprised everyone.
gaps.hint: refers to the whole previous clause
gaps.explanation: 'Which' can refer to a whole idea ('he passed first time'); this non-defining use never takes 'that'.

gaps.sentence: ___ surprised me most was his calm.
gaps.hint: 'what' = the thing that; the sentence has no other subject
gaps.explanation: 'What' means 'the thing that' and acts as subject: 'What surprised me most ...' — 'that' cannot introduce this nominal clause.
